sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Jev enables efficient decision-making with large language models (LLMs) through typed querying primitives, allowing the same semantic state to be expressed in different formats, such as binary and multiple-choice queries. However, the consistency of decisions across primitives has not been systematically evaluated. This work introduces PrimaCons, a four-axis benchmark for assessing cross-primitive consistency while preserving the semantics of the query. Evaluations across three Jev sizes reveal consistency violations across all four axes. Our analysis shows that these violations follow systematic patterns and that cross-primitive discrepancies predict decision failure with a ROC-AUC of 0.91. To mitigate these inconsistencies, we propose the Cross-Primitive Residual Calibrator (CPRC), which attaches a lightweight residual network to a frozen backbone and jointly optimizes predictive accuracy and cross-primitive consistency. Under a leave-one-domain-out protocol, CPRC reduces cross-primitive inconsistency by 58.57% and improves accuracy by +2.97%., demonstrating its effectiveness in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Our findings establish cross-primitive consistency as a key dimension for evaluating Jev and provide a practical approach to improving the reliability of its decisions. Code and benchmark is available at https://github.com/67L1/PrimaCons-CRPR.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Jev enables efficient decision-making with large language models (LLMs) through typed querying primitives, allowing the same semantic state to be expressed in different formats, such as binary and multiple-choice queries. However, the consistency of decisions across primitives has not been systematically evaluated. This work introduces PRIMACONS, four-axis benchmark for assessing crossprimitive consistency while preserving the semantics of the query. Evaluations across three Jev sizes reveal consistency violations across all four axes. Our analysis shows that these violations follow systematic patterns and that cross-primitive discrepancies predict decision failure with ROC-AUC of 0.91. To mitigate these inconsistencies, we propose the Cross-Primitive Residual Calibrator (CPRC), which attaches lightweight residual network to frozen backbone and jointly optimizes predictive accuracy and cross-primitive consistency. Under leave-one-domain-out protocol, CPRC reduces cross-primitive inconsistency by 58.57% and improves accuracy by +2.97%., demonstrating its effectiveness in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Our findings establish cross-primitive consistency as key dimension for evaluating Jev and provide practical approach to improving the reliability of its decisions. 1. Introduction Jev has attracted growing interest as an approach to structured decision-making with LLMs. Recent studies have investigated its capabilities, implementations, and extensions [1, 12, 16, 33], alongside emerging applications in clinical evaluation [11, 15, 20, 41, 45] and safety moderation [31, 42, 47, 58]. Unlike conventional LLM applications that generate free-form text, Jev represents decision tasks through typed querying primitives and obtains structured predictions directly from model outputs. For example, Noul formulates binary decision, whereas Choice 1Corresponding Author. Figure 1. An example of cross-primitive inconsistency. presents multiple candidate answers. These primitives provide different interfaces for expressing decision tasks, allowing model to return structured outcomes without generating and subsequently parsing natural language response. This design reduces inference overhead and supports efficient decision-making across diverse applications. The combination of structured outputs and efficient inference has made Jev an increasingly relevant approach to deploying LLMs in decision-oriented settings. Research on Jev has primarily examined its predictive capabilities, calibration, robustness, and performance on specific tasks [11, 40, 42, 53]. However, evaluating decisions under single querying primitive leaves an important aspect of model behavior unexamined: whether the same semantic state yields consistent decisions when expressed through different primitives. This issue is closely related to consistency in LLMs, which has been studied under various forms of input variation [3, 13, 44, 50], but cross-primitive consistency in Jev remains unexplored. Unlike comparisons between arbitrary inputs, this setting requires the underlying decision semantics to remain fixed while the querying interface changes. When the resulting decisions disagree, the discrepancy cannot be explained by change in the intended task alone. As illustrated in Fig. 1, Noul query returns False (the response is factual), whereas semantically equivalent Choice query selects Hallucinated (the response is hallucinated). Such contradictions reveal dimension of decision reliability that conventional accuracy evaluations cannot capture. systematic investigation of 1 cross-primitive consistency is therefore necessary to understand how querying interfaces affect Jevs decisions and whether the resulting inconsistencies can be mitigated. To enable such an investigation, we introduce PRIMACONS, benchmark that evaluates cross-primitive consistency along four complementary axes: Complement Consistency, Label Hierarchy Consistency, Abstention Alignment Consistency, and Label-Description Consistency. These axes examine decision invariance under binary isomorphism, taxonomic coherence, procedure invariance, description invariance, and projection invariance, respectively. PRIMACONS is constructed from HaluEval [25], PKUSafeRLHF [21], AbstentionBench [23], and AG News [67], with separate calibration and test splits. By preserving the semantics of the queries while varying the relevant querying primitive or presentation choice, PRIMACONS supports controlled evaluation across multiple forms of decision inconsistency. We quantify discrepancies using probability gaps, total variation, and complementary decisionlevel metrics. Evaluations of JevK5-2B, JevK5-4B, and JevK5-9B reveal consistency violations across all four axes. Specifically, further analysis identifies the following four recurring patterns: cross-primitive discrepancies predict decision failure with ROC-AUC of 0.91; inconsistency increases with finer label granularity and is accompanied by probability-mass inflation; the magnitude and direction of disagreement depend on the querying primitive; and text augmentation can exacerbate cross-primitive discrepancies. These findings demonstrate that the cross-primitive inconsistency is systematic and associated with identifiable properties of the decision task and its formulation. Building on these findings, we propose the Cross-Primitive Residual Calibrator (CPRC) to mitigate cross-primitive inconsistency. CPRC freezes the backbone and attaches lightweight residual network that predicts logit corrections, adjusting decision distributions without updating the full model. Its training objective combines cross-entropy with consistency penalty, jointly encouraging predictive accuracy and alignment across semantically equivalent queries. We evaluate CPRC using leave-one-domain-out (LODO) protocol to assess its effectiveness on both observed and held-out domains. In the in-domain setting, CPRC reduces Gn+,n from 0.183 to 0.087 (-52.6%) and improves accuracy from 77.67% to 98.48% (+20.81%). Under LODO it achieves reduction of (pr, pn) from evaluation, 0.439 to 0.182 (-58.6%), and improves accuracy on raw labels from 84.90% to 87.42% (+2.52%). These results demonstrate that cross-primitive consistency can be improved through lightweight calibration while maintaining or enhancing predictive performance across domains. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce PRIMACONS, four-axis benchmark for systematically evaluating cross-primitive consistency in Jev while controlling for the semantics of the queries. We conduct an empirical study across 3 Jev models, revealing consistency violations across all axes and characterizing systematicity, granularity amplification, primitive asymmetry, and sensitivity to text augmentation. We propose CPRC, lightweight calibration method that combines the predictive supervision with crossprimitive consistency objective, improving decision consistency and accuracy across different domains. 2. PRIMACONS This section introduces PRIMACONS, Cross-Primitive Consistency Benchmark, designed to evaluate Jevs internal consistency when semantic states remain constant while calling primitives change. PRIMACONS encompasses four test scenarios, each targeting distinct dimension of consistency: i) complement consistency (2.1), ii) label hierarchy consistency (2.2), iii) abstention alignment consistency (2.3), and iv) label-description consistency (2.4). 2.1. Axis I: Complement Consistency PRIMACONSs axis tests whether positive and negative inquiries about the same proposition yield complementary probabilities, preserving binary isomorphism. To evaluate this, we adopt HaluEval [25], hallucination benchmark in which model must judge whether response contains hallucinated content given provided context. We split it into balanced 6,000-sample calibration set and 6,000-sample test set. For each record, we construct state si by concatenating the provided context and target response. We then subject it to three primitives: positive Noul (querying the presence of hallucination), reversed Noul (querying factual correctness), and binary Choice. We quantify consistency by the probability gap among the three views. 2.2. Axis II: Label Hierarchy Consistency PRIMACONSs axis II tests whether the coarse-grained decision of sample agrees with what its fine-grained category decisions jointly imply. We adopt PKU-SafeRLHF [21], safety alignment dataset that labels each text as toxic or not across multiple granularities. We retain the samples labeled as unsafe, and select 6,000 calibration samples and 4,000 test samples. We employ the original 12 fine-grained safety categories, which are then paired two-by-two into mediumlevel parent categories and ultimately projected to single coarse label of whether the sample is safe. Instead of changing textual phrasing, we perturb the decision granularity. We quantify consistency between the fine-grained predictions at different levels and the coarse-grained predictions. 2.3. Axis III: Abstention Alignment Consistency PRIMACONSs axis III investigates whether offering an unable to answer option alters the models confidence 2 about answerability. To assess this, we employ AbstentionBench [23], an benchmark in which model is given context and question and judge the questions answerability. We establish 6,000-sample calibration set and 6,000sample test set, each covering an equal number of answerable and unanswerable samples. We test two primitives: three-option Choice and binary Noul. For answerable questions, the Choice options contain the correct answer, distractor, and an unable to answer option. For unanswerable questions, they contain two distractors and an unable to answer option. For both types, Noul queries whether the question can be answered. We evaluate consistency by computing the probability gap and decision conflict rate between Choices and Nouls abstention selections. 2.4. Axis IV: Label-Description Consistency PRIMACONSs axis IV measures distribution robustness when choice labels are augmented with text descriptions. Since the textual state is unchanged, neither description augmentation nor primitive should shift the distribution. Adopting the four AG News categories [67], we construct 6,000-sample calibration set and 6,000-sample test set. For each sample, we quantify consistency at two levels: i) between Choice primitive with raw category labels and one with description-augmented labels, and ii) between Choices probability distribution and normalized distribution derived from four category-specific Noul queries. We measure their consistency with Total Variation (T ). 3. Consistency on PRIMACONS 3.1. Evaluation Metrics We conduct experiments on JevK5-2B, JevK5-4B and JevK5-9B using the calibration split of PRIMACONS. For each evaluation axis, consistency metrics are introduced, with the exhaustive equations delegated to the Appendix. Axis I: Complement Consistency. Axis IV: Label-Description Consistency. Description Invariance requires that rephrasing the options should not change the decision distribution. If two labels denote the same category, augmenting them with descriptive text should preserve JevK5s judgment. As shown in Table 4, adding descriptive text shifts the Choice distribution (T (pr, pd) = 0.1013). It indicates that even within the same primitive, the neutral descriptive text perturbs the decision distribution. Another requirement concerns the Projection Invariance between binary and multi-class views. Each category-specific Noul query answers binary question and thus lives in {0, 1}K, whereas the Choice returns point in the probability simplex K1. Normalizing the Noul probabilities is projection from the former to the latter, and the projected distribution should recover the same decision state as the one reported by Choice. As shown in Table 4, shifting from Choice to the Noul triggers relocation of probability mass, yielding (pr, pn) = 0.2405. Because JevK5 already violates description invariance, the descriptive text further amplifies this drift, raising the gap to (pd, pn) = 0.2694 when the same comparison is made with the description-augmented Choice. This gap indicates that the decision state is not preserved under the {0, 1}K K1 projection. To further investigate the violation of Description Invariance and Projection Invariance, we examine the samplewise probability distributions across different primitives and choices. As shown in Fig. 6, Choice and Noul probabilities should coincide on the diagonal = if both invariances held. Instead, the predictions deviate markedly, exhibiting an asymmetric crossing pattern: when the Choice probability is low, the Noul probability tends to be higher, whereas when the Choice probability is high, Noul becomes more conservative. This indicates that the two primitives interpret the same probability space differently. Beyond measuring the consistency metrics of each axis, we additionally report accuracy. In-Domain Evaluation. Table 5 shows the CPRCs results on Axis I, II, and III. CPRC mitigates cross-primitive inconsistency across all three axes. For example, on JevK5-2B in Axis I, Gn+,n drops from 0.183 to 0.087 (-52.56%) while Choice accuracy rises from 65.03% to 79.00% (+13.97%). On JevK5-4B in Axis II, the fine-level divergence DF drops from 0.633 to 0.355 (-43.95%) while accuracy rises from 95.20% to 99.65% (+4.45%). On JevK5-2B in Axis II, DM drops from 0.481 to 0.130 (-73.03%) while accuracy rises from 77.67% to 98.48% (+20.81%). Out-of-Domain Generalization. To evaluate whether CPRC learns fundamental corrections rather than memorizing domain-specific statistics, we test it under the LODO protocol, with Axis IV as the unseen target domain. The results show that CPRC generalizes its consistency improvements to this unseen domain  (Table 6)  . For example, on JevK5-2B, (pr, pn) drops from 0.439 to 0.182 (-58.57%) while raw-label accuracy rises from 84.90% to 87.42% (+2.97%). The same model also reduces (pd, pn) from 0.474 to 0.237 (-49.98%) while description-augmented accuracy rises from 86.80% to 87.90% (+1.27%). On JevK5-9B, (pr, pn) drops from 0.225 to 0.094 (-58.42%) while raw-label accuracy rises from 88.02% to 89.75% (+1.96%). Averaged over 6,000 test instances, CPRC introduces only +0.75% additional latency overhead, which is negligible. 5. Related Work System-One Decision Model reduces the cost and improves the speed of using LLMs as decision models through System One-style single-pass inference. Existing Jevrelated methods are broadly categorized into three streams. The first category is Empirical Evaluation and Capability Distillation. These methods benchmark system limits or distill decision priors to optimize inference efficiency, e.g., probing zero-shot reasoning boundaries across diverse tasks [10, 30, 48, 65] and building Jev-style decision models via direct logit readout or low-rank adaptation [16, 32, 33, 39, 56, 60]. The second category is Domain-Specific Adaptation. These methods fine-tune decision layers to target specialized scenarios, e.g., automating clinical and medical evaluations [15, 41] and integrating multilingual or normative knowledge [5, 27, 59]. The third category is Adversarial Vulnerability and Safety Assessment. These methods perturb inputs or exploit contextual shifts to expose decision fragility, e.g., executing blackbox adversarial edits and prompt injections [19, 31, 61] and demonstrating susceptibility to natural context flips [63], alongside deploying them as zero-shot safety detectors [18]. Despite delineating external performance boundaries, these methods only evaluate input-output pairs without verifying internal coherence, introducing reliability risks when semantically equivalent queries yield contradictory decisions. Consistency of LLMs refers to the invariance of their outputs under semantically equivalent inputs. Existing studies are broadly categorized into three streams. The first category is Contextual and Semantic Perturbation Robustness. These methods inject surface-level noise to expose output instability, e.g., mutating prompts while preserving logical semantics to detect behavioral drift [8, 9, 14, 29, 52, 54] and evaluating reasoning degradation under adversarial inputs, irrelevant distractors, or counterfactual evidence [24, 35, 43, 46, 64, 66, 68, 69]. The second category is Internal Representation and Quantization Sensitivity. These methods perturb weights and activations to analyze collapse during low-bit compression, e.g., isolating activation spikes and positional encoding artifacts [6, 17, 22, 49], tracking how quantization shrinks decision margins [34, 34, 38, 51, 55], and probing rescaling invariance, feedback exposure, and value-magnitude sensitivity in low-bit rounding [2, 26, 28, 62]. The third category is Intermediate Reasoning Trace Faithfulness. These methods audit multi-step generation pipelines to detect logical disconnects, e.g., exposing rationales that fabricate evidence for predetermined answers [4, 64], optimizing intermediate token probabilities via consistency decoding or confidence-weighted aggregation, probing commitment misalignment [28], answer-reasoning disconnect [9, 37, 38], and semantic drift [7, 36, 57]. Our work builds on the unique architecture of decision models, in which the context is decoupled from the querying primitive. It raises question that single-primitive architecture cannot capture: whether the same state yields consistent decision across primitives, which directly reflects the models decision reliability. We quantify this crossprimitive consistency, grounding each axis in distinct theoretical requirement (binary isomorphism, taxonomic coherence, procedure invariance, description invariance, and projection invariance) and propose CPRC, calibrator that aligns the probability distributions across primitives. 6. Conclusion System-One decision models bypass reasoning to accelerate inference. Their reliability is therefore hard to audit, yet it can still be assessed through consistency. Cross-primitive consistency offers one such lens. Therefore, we introduce PRIMACONS to quantify it, revealing that current decision models violate different invariants across complementary, hierarchical, abstention, and label-description dimensions. To mitigate this inconsistency, we propose CPRC, which appends lightweight residual network and optimizes the network while keeping the backbone frozen via joint consistency objective. Validated under an LODO protocol, CPRC curtails inconsistency and boosts accuracy across unseen domains. We hope this work offers lens for assessing decision-model reliability and that the proposed calibrator helps make such models deployable in high-risk scenarios.
